claim: The inner ear is an attractive model for studying spatiotemporally controlled cell specification and differentiation alongside morphogenesis because it is accessible to manipulation and undergoes dynamic self-organization.
source: The inner ear is an attractive model to take on this challenge since it is accessible to manipulation, and it undergoes dynamic self-organization.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the inner ear as a model system, drawing on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The inner ear contains a manageable number of distinct cell types that develop rapidly on an organized schedule to generate the functional units of the mature organ.
source: It contains a manageable number of distinct cell types, which develop rapidly on an organized schedule to generate the functional units of the mature organ – the sensory patches.
evidence: This is a general statement about the characteristics of inner ear development, based on established knowledge.

claim: The key cell types of the inner ear (supporting cells, hair cells, and sensory neurons) originate early during embryonic development from progenitors located in the otic vesicle.
source: The key cell types of the inner ear, the supporting cells and the hair cells of the sensory patches, and the sensory neurons that innervate them, originate early during embryonic development from progenitors located in the otic vesicle, a 3D-structure arising from the otic placode adjacent to the developing hindbrain (Durruthy-Durruthy et al., 2014; Raft et al., 2007; Sapède et al., 2012; Satoh and Fekete, 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The otic vesicle is a 3D-structure arising from the otic placode adjacent to the developing hindbrain.
source: The key cell types of the inner ear, the supporting cells and the hair cells of the sensory patches, and the sensory neurons that innervate them, originate early during embryonic development from progenitors located in the otic vesicle, a 3D-structure arising from the otic placode adjacent to the developing hindbrain (Durruthy-Durruthy et al., 2014; Raft et al., 2007; Sapède et al., 2012; Satoh and Fekete, 2005)
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the otic vesicle supported by citations.

claim: Inner ear cell types are easy to score by morphology, position and specific markers.
source: and they are easy to score by morphology, position and specific markers (Haddon and Lewis, 1996; Raft and Groves, 2015; Whitfield, 2015; Wu and Kelley, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: atoh1 is required for hair cell formation.
source: Neuronal vs. sensory specification is achieved through well-defined bHLH transcription factors: atoh1 for hair cell formation (Millimaki et al., 2007; Bermingham et al., 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: neurog1 is required for sensory neuron determination.
source: neurog1 for sensory neuron determination (Andermann et al., 2002; Ma et al., 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: neuroD is required for sensory neuron differentiation and survival.
source: and neuroD for sensory neuron differentiation and survival (Jahan et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Signals arising in the surrounding tissues regionalize the otic vesicle along axes.
source: Signals arising in the surrounding tissues regionalize the otic vesicle along axes (Maier and Whitfield, 2014; Radosevic et al., 2011; Riccomagno et al., 2002, 2005; Sapède and Pujades, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The first delamination events of neuroblasts occur at 18 hpf in the most anterolateral region of the otic floor.
source: We observed the first delamination events at 18 hpf in the most anterolateral region of the otic floor (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a–a').
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation from in vivo imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The neuroblast delamination domain expands towards middle and posterior regions with cells delaminating very close to the neural tube.
source: This domain expanded towards middle and posterior regions with cells delaminating very close to the neural tube (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b–c´), as had been described by analysis of serial transverse sections from 22 hpf onwards (Haddon and Lewis, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data and corroborated by a citation to prior work.

claim: The delamination domain expands quickly from anterolateral to posteromedial.
source: Segmentation of the epithelial neuroD-domain allowed us to illustrate the quick expansion of this territory from anterolateral to posteromedial (Figure 1b–d), and when comparing three different embryos this emerges as a common trend (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This claim is based on segmentation analysis of imaging data from multiple embryos.

claim: The neuroblast cell body moves basally in less than one hour after undergoing apical constriction.
source: Segmentation of individual cells -delineation of the cell contours by computational tools- when transiting from the epithelium to the SAG showed that the neuroblast cell body moves basally in less than one hour after undergoing apical constriction (see red cell in Video 2; Figure 1e–g').
evidence: This claim is based on cell segmentation analysis from imaging data.

claim: Neighboring neuroblasts often delaminate consecutively to accumulate in the SAG.
source: Neighboring neuroblasts often delaminate consecutively to accumulate in the SAG, which quickly becomes an adjacent compact mass extending beneath the ventral floor of the otic vesicle along the anteroposterior axis by 22 hpf (Figure 1h–i; Video 1).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from imaging data.

claim: The SAG becomes an adjacent compact mass extending beneath the ventral floor of the otic vesicle along the anteroposterior axis by 22 hpf.
source: Neighboring neuroblasts often delaminate consecutively to accumulate in the SAG, which quickly becomes an adjacent compact mass extending beneath the ventral floor of the otic vesicle along the anteroposterior axis by 22 hpf (Figure 1h–i; Video 1).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from imaging data.

claim: As early as 20 hpf the SAG rudiment already innervates the different maculae.
source: As early as 20 hpf the SAG rudiment already innervates the different maculae
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge or prior observations.

claim: By 48 hpf the SAG is composed of two segregated neuronal populations that display the same molecular signature but innervate different sensory patches.
source: and by 48 hpf the SAG is composed of two segregated neuronal populations that although displaying the same molecular signature innervate different sensory patches (Sapède and Pujades, 2010; Zecca et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Within six hours after the first delamination events, a big bulk of neuroblasts delaminates.
source: Analysis of the dynamics of this process revealed that once the first delamination events are observed, delamination occurs massively. The lineage tree shows that within six hours a big bulk of neuroblasts delaminates (see white, yellow and orange lines in Figure 2a corresponding to single delaminated neuroblasts)
evidence: This claim is based on lineage tree analysis from imaging data.

claim: Many neuroblasts can divide after exiting the epithelium.
source: and many neuroblasts can divide after exiting (see lines branching in Figure 2a) as previously described (Vemaraju et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on lineage tree analysis and corroborated by a citation.

claim: Neuroblasts delaminate randomly in space and time.
source: The first observation was that neuroblasts delaminated randomly in space and time (see intermingled colors of the reconstructed cell centers in Figure 2b)
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of reconstructed cell centers from imaging data.

claim: The organization of neuroblasts within the SAG relies on the delamination order, with delaminated cells aggregating laterally to the preexisting ganglion.
source: but their organization within the SAG relies on the delamination order as delaminated cells aggregate laterally to the preexisting ganglion (Video 3), thereby generating a mediolateral (ML) growth pattern with early-delaminated cells (white) located more medially than late-delaminated ones (red) (Figure 2c–c´; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b for additional analysis).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of cell tracking data from imaging.

claim: Early-delaminated neuroblasts are located more medially than late-delaminated ones in the SAG, generating a mediolateral growth pattern.
source: but their organization within the SAG relies on the delamination order as delaminated cells aggregate laterally to the preexisting ganglion (Video 3), thereby generating a mediolateral (ML) growth pattern with early-delaminated cells (white) located more medially than late-delaminated ones (red) (Figure 2c–c´; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b for additional analysis).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of cell tracking data from imaging.

claim: As the inner ear grows and undergoes morphogenesis, the SAG becomes squeezed between the ventromedial wall of the ear and the neural tube, converting its organization from mediolateral to dorsoventral.
source: While the inner ear grows and undergoes morphogenesis, the SAG becomes squeezed in the space between the ventromedial wall of the ear and the neural tube, such that its organization is gradually converted from ML to dorsoventral (DV), with early-delaminated sensory neurons located in close contact with the neural tube (Video 3; Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from imaging data over time.

claim: The time of neuroblast delamination foreshadows the mediolateral gradient of neuronal differentiation in the SAG.
source: Thus, the time of neuroblast delamination foreshadows the ML gradient of neuronal differentiation in the SAG.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed relationship between delamination time and cell position.

claim: Neuroblasts from the anterior portion of the SAG delaminate from the anterolateral floor of the otic vesicle.
source: We found that the relative position of progenitors foresees their final location in the SAG: neuroblasts from the anterior portion of the SAG delaminated from the anterolateral floor of the otic vesicle, while the ones of the posterior SAG derived from the posteromedial otic epithelium (Video 4).
evidence: This claim is based on backtracking analysis of neuroblasts from imaging data.

claim: Neuroblasts from the posterior portion of the SAG delaminate from the posteromedial otic epithelium.
source: We found that the relative position of progenitors foresees their final location in the SAG: neuroblasts from the anterior portion of the SAG delaminated from the anterolateral floor of the otic vesicle, while the ones of the posterior SAG derived from the posteromedial otic epithelium (Video 4).
evidence: This claim is based on backtracking analysis of neuroblasts from imaging data.

claim: The anteroposterior coordinates of neuroblast delamination generally define their relative anteroposterior position within the SAG.
source: We observed that the anteroposterior (AP) coordinates of neuroblasts delamination (see differently colored epithelial cell center populations in Figure 2d) generally defined their relative AP position within the SAG (Figure 2e–e'; Video 5; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–d' for additional analysis).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of cell position data from imaging.

claim: Progenitors delaminating within similar spatial regions along the AP axis maintain similar relative positions later on.
source: These data show that progenitors delaminating within similar spatial regions along the AP axis maintain similar relative positions later on, and indeed the analysis of their trajectories indicates that cells, while in the otic epithelium, maintain their neighbor relationships.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the trajectory analysis of cells.

claim: No correlation was observed between mediolateral coordinates of neuroblast delamination and their position within the SAG.
source: No such correlation was observed regarding the ML axis, because cells that were originally separated in the epithelium were found close in the SAG (Figure 2f–g'; Video 5), suggesting that the AP and time cues prevail.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of cell position data from imaging.

claim: The place and order of neuroblast delamination prefigure their neuronal (functional) identity within the SAG.
source: These findings establish a link between the place and order of neuroblast delamination and their neuronal (functional) identity within the SAG
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed relationships between delamination parameters and SAG organization.

claim: There is spatial and temporal regulation in the otic epithelium of the fate and exit of SAG neuroblasts.
source: and suggest the existence of a spatial and temporal regulation in the otic epithelium of the fate and exit of SAG neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed patterns.

claim: One third of the analyzed neuroblasts divided after delamination.
source: one third divided after delamination (n = 40 orange cells in Figure 3a; Figure 3—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: This claim is based on clonal analysis from imaging data.

claim: One third of the analyzed neuroblasts did not divide within the analyzed time interval.
source: and a similar fraction of neuroblasts did not divide within this time interval (n = 34 blue cells in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is based on clonal analysis from imaging data.

claim: Cell position within the otic epithelium is not relevant for neuroblast cell division behaviors.
source: Thus, cell position within the otic epithelium is not relevant for these cell division behaviors because no specific spatial distribution can be observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the spatial distribution analysis of dividing cells.

claim: Cell division and delamination are independent events.
source: In addition, cell division and delamination are independent events, in contrast to what was proposed for epithelial invagination of the Drosophila tracheal placode (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed lack of correlation between division and delamination, contrasted with a cited example.

claim: In most cases, sister cell delaminations happen within a two hours interval.
source: Neuroblasts dividing before delamination give rise to two daughter cells that will delaminate (Figure 3a–c). In most cases, sister cell delaminations happened within a two hours interval
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of sister cell delamination timing from imaging data.

claim: In a few cases the time of delamination between two sister cells can be as long as seven hours.
source: however in a few cases the time of delamination between two sister cells can be as long as seven hours (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of sister cell delamination timing from imaging data.

claim: Epithelial neuroblasts' divisions give rise to cells that will delaminate.
source: Overall, these analyses suggest that (i) epithelial neuroblasts' divisions give rise to cells that will delaminate (Figure 3c)
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the clonal analysis.

claim: Cell division is not necessary as a trigger for delamination.
source: and (ii) cell division is not necessary as a trigger for delamination.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that some cells delaminate without dividing.

claim: About 25% of total otic cells at 18 hpf exit by delamination between 18 hpf and 22 hpf.
source: Due to the massive cell delamination in a relatively short time (more than 150 delamination events in the period 18-26 hpf), the neuronal progenitor domain undergoes dramatic size and shape changes (Figure 3d, compare the territory containing orange cell circles at 18 hpf and 26 hpf), as described by Haddon and Lewis (1996). Upon delamination a large amount of cells exits from the otic epithelium: about 25% of total otic cells at 18 hpf are lost by delamination between 18 hpf and 22 hpf.
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of delamination events from imaging data.

claim: The neuronal progenitor domain undergoes dramatic size and shape changes due to massive cell delamination.
source: Due to the massive cell delamination in a relatively short time (more than 150 delamination events in the period 18-26 hpf), the neuronal progenitor domain undergoes dramatic size and shape changes (Figure 3d, compare the territory containing orange cell circles at 18 hpf and 26 hpf), as described by Haddon and Lewis (1996).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from imaging data and corroborated by a citation.

claim: The exit of neuroblasts and the growth of the vesicle progressively restrict the progenitor field to a more lateral region of the ventral floor of the vesicle.
source: The exit of neuroblasts and the growth of the vesicle are part of the morphogenetic processes that progressively restricted the progenitor field to a more lateral region of the ventral floor of the vesicle (orange cell centers in Figure 3d, 26 hpf).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observations of progenitor domain changes over time.

claim: In the fish, the first hair cells differentiate while neuronal precursors are still delaminating.
source: However, one difference is that in the fish the first hair cells differentiate while neuronal precursors are still delaminating
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about zebrafish development.

claim: Hair cells continue to be produced throughout life in fish.
source: and that hair cells continue to be produced throughout life (Haddon and Lewis, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The first hair cells to arise (tether cells) constitute the posterior pole of each of the maculae.
source: The first hair cells to arise -the so called tether cells (Riley et al., 1997)- constituted the posterior pole of each of the maculae (white-dotted cells in Figure 4a–c; Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,c)
evidence: This claim is based on observations from imaging data and includes a citation.

claim: Tether cells prefigure the position of the sensory patches within the otic vesicle.
source: and prefigured the position of these sensory patches within the otic vesicle (Video 6).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from imaging data.

claim: The two sensory patches gradually increase their size by incorporating differentiated hair cells at their anterior pole with a specific pattern.
source: Next, these two sensory patches gradually increased their size incorporating differentiated hair cells at their anterior pole with a specific pattern (see color-coded cell centers in Figure 4b–c; Video 6; ID Dataset: 140507aX; and see Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,c for additional samples exhibiting the same pattern).
evidence: This claim is based on tracking of differentiated hair cells from imaging data.

claim: Once hair cells differentiate they become postmitotic.
source: Once hair cells differentiate they become postmitotic (Video 6).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from imaging data showing no division of differentiated hair cells.

claim: The anterior and posterior maculae develop asynchronously, with the incorporation of new hair cells being delayed in the posterior macula.
source: AM and PM develop asynchronously, with the incorporation of new hair cells being delayed in the PM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Sapède and Pujades, 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from imaging data and corroborated by a citation.

claim: A specific pool of neuronal progenitors switches its fate to hair cells of the posterior macula upon abrogation of neurog1 function.
source: Previous findings indicated that a specific pool of neuronal progenitors switches its fate to hair cells of the PM upon abrogation of neurog1 function (Sapède et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the absence of neurog1, sensory neurons do not form and supernumerary hair cells are produced in the posterior macula.
source: In the absence of neurog1, sensory neurons do not form and supernumerary hair cells are produced in the PM (Figure 4f–h; Video 6).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from imaging data of MO-neurog1 embryos.

claim: The overall spatial pattern of hair cell generation in the anterior and posterior maculae is very similar between control and morphant embryos.
source: Tracking the differentiated hair cells allowed us to compare the dynamics of sensory development at the single-cell level: the overall spatial pattern of hair cell generation in the AM/PM was very similar between control and morphant embryos (compare Figure 4b–c with g–h)
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of imaging data between control and MO-neurog1 embryos.

claim: The kinetics of hair cell production in the posterior macula differs between control and MO-neurog1 embryos due to a boost of differentiation from 34 hpf onwards.
source: however the kinetics of hair cell production in the PM differed due to a boost of differentiation in MO-neurog1 from 34 hpf onwards (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of imaging data between control and MO-neurog1 embryos.

claim: All supernumerary hair cells in the MO-neurog1 originate from newly differentiated cells, not from differentiated hair cells re-entering the cell cycle.
source: All supernumerary hair cells in the MO-neurog1 originate from newly differentiated cells, and not from differentiated hair cells re-entering the cell cycle (Video 6).
evidence: This claim is based on tracking analysis from imaging data.

claim: Progenitors for hair cells of the posterior macula are distributed over the ventromedial domain of the otic vesicle at early stages of embryonic development.
source: 3D-reconstructions revealed that progenitors for hair cells of the PM were distributed over the ventromedial domain of the otic vesicle at early stages of embryonic development (see color-coded cell centers in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: This claim is based on backtracking analysis from imaging data.

claim: Upon neurog1 inhibition the hair cell progenitor pool expands along the anteroposterior dimension and allocates more medially.
source: and that upon neurog1 inhibition the hair cell progenitor pool expanded along the anteroposterior dimension allocating more medially (ID Dataset: 140519aX; Figure 4i, Video 7).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of progenitor maps between control and MO-neurog1 embryos.

claim: The position of hair cell progenitors foreshadows the organization of differentiated cells within the sensory patch.
source: Furthermore, the position of hair cell progenitors foreshadows the organization of differentiated cells within the sensory patch, demonstrating that otic epithelial cells did not rearrange during early stages of hair cell differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed relationship between progenitor position and differentiated cell organization.

claim: Otic epithelial cells do not rearrange during early stages of hair cell differentiation.
source: Furthermore, the position of hair cell progenitors foreshadows the organization of differentiated cells within the sensory patch, demonstrating that otic epithelial cells did not rearrange during early stages of hair cell differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed maintenance of relative positions.

claim: The progenitor maps for hair cells and neurons at the onset of hair cell differentiation (24 hpf) are largely segregated with a small region of putative overlap.
source: Finally, our analysis allowed us to compare the progenitor maps for hair cells and neurons at the onset of hair cell differentiation (24 hpf): they were largely segregated with a small region of putative overlap (Video 8), consistent with the existence of a pool of dual progenitors (Sapède et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of progenitor maps from imaging data and is consistent with a cited prior finding.

claim: Cells within the non-sensory domain actively proliferate.
source: Cells within the non-sensory domain actively proliferated (Figure 5a–c; Video 9)
evidence: This claim is based on lineage reconstruction analysis from imaging data.

claim: Half of the analyzed cells in the ventral region do not divide and some differentiate into hair cells.
source: in contrast, half of the analyzed cells in the ventral region did not divide and some differentiated into hair cells (Figure 5d–f; Video 9)
evidence: This claim is based on lineage reconstruction analysis from imaging data.

claim: Once hair cell progenitors are committed they divide less.
source: in contrast, half of the analyzed cells in the ventral region did not divide and some differentiated into hair cells (Figure 5d–f; Video 9), suggesting that once hair cell progenitors are committed they divide less.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed lower division rate in the sensory domain.

claim: The non-sensory domain is less compacted than the sensory domain despite displaying higher proliferative activity.
source: Interestingly, even though the non-sensory domain displayed higher proliferative activity, it was less compacted (note neighboring reconstructed cell centers are more spaced in Figure 5a–b than in d–e), supporting the idea that it contributes to the overall growth of the vesicle during this time window.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of cell spacing from imaging data.

claim: The non-sensory domain contributes to the overall growth of the vesicle.
source: Interestingly, even though the non-sensory domain displayed higher proliferative activity, it was less compacted (note neighboring reconstructed cell centers are more spaced in Figure 5a–b than in d–e), supporting the idea that it contributes to the overall growth of the vesicle during this time window.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed proliferation and spacing patterns.

claim: Similar cell behaviors and cell organization are observed in the MO-neurog1 with no increase in proliferative activity in the sensory domain.
source: Similar cell behaviors and cell organization were observed in the MO-neurog1 with no increase in proliferative activity in the sensory domain (Figure 5g–l)
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of lineage reconstruction data between control and MO-neurog1 embryos.

claim: Upon neurog1 abrogation, hair cell progenitors do not divide more actively.
source: revealing that upon neurog1 abrogation hair cell progenitors do not divide more actively
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed lack of increased proliferation in MO-neurog1.

claim: Supernumerary hair cells in MO-neurog1 derive either from expansion of the progenitor pool or from precocious differentiation of progenitors.
source: and therefore supernumerary hair cells derive either from expansion of the progenitor pool, or from precocious differentiation of progenitors.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed lack of increased proliferation.

claim: In MO-neurog1, the number of cells in the otic vesicle is greatly increased compared to control.
source: While upon neurog1 abrogation the number of cells was greatly increased (Figure 5o; control = 384 ± 17 cells n = 3 vs. neurog1hi5109/hi5109 = 479 ± 14 cells n = 3 or MO-neurog1 = 506 ± 14 cells n = 2)
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of cell numbers from imaging data.

claim: The global pattern of cell densities does not change between control and MO-neurog1 embryos.
source: the global pattern of cell densities did not change: cells in either condition are most densely packed in the anterolateral and ventral region and most spaced in the dorsal domain (see red and blue cells in Figure 5m–n; Video 10).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of local cell density estimates from imaging data.

claim: The impact of non-delaminated cells on the compaction of the otic epithelium is low.
source: This suggests that the impact of non-delaminated cells in the compaction of the otic epithelium is low.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed maintenance of cell density patterns.

claim: The otic vesicles of MO-neurog1 are larger than control ones.
source: Thus, if in the MO-neurog1 cell density is not altered but cell numbers are higher in the vesicle, the volume of the otic structure should be larger than the control one. Indeed, when assessing the volumes by 3D-point-cloud segmentation the otic vesicles of MO-neurog1 were larger than the control ones (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c–e).
evidence: This claim is based on volume measurements from imaging data.

claim: The otic epithelium is a heterogeneous tissue where proliferative activity and cell compaction differ between sensory and non-sensory domains during the generation of neurosensory cellular elements.
source: Altogether these results show that the otic epithelium is a heterogeneous tissue, where proliferative activity and cell compaction differ between sensory and non-sensory domains during the generation of the neurosensory cellular elements.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from multiple observations about proliferation and cell density.

claim: Neuronal specification is concomitant with proliferation (before/after delamination).
source: To assure the robust outcome of a functional inner ear, with sensory patches containing the precise number of mechanosensory hair cells properly innervated by sensory neurons arranged in a precise topology (Video 11), the developmental strategy used by distinct progenitor populations differs: neuronal specification is concomitant with proliferation (before/after delamination)
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the observed division behaviors of neuroblasts.

claim: Hair cell specification and differentiation lead to postmitotic cells.
source: while hair cell specification and differentiation lead to postmitotic cells indicating that the final number of sensory cells relies on the control of the progenitor pool.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the observed postmitotic nature of differentiated hair cells.

claim: The final number of sensory cells relies on the control of the progenitor pool.
source: while hair cell specification and differentiation lead to postmitotic cells indicating that the final number of sensory cells relies on the control of the progenitor pool.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the postmitotic nature of hair cells.

claim: Although the otic vesicle undergoes morphogenesis and cells extensively proliferate, progenitors do not rearrange within the epithelium during early stages of hair cell differentiation.
source: Interestingly, the position of hair cell progenitors foreshadows the organization of differentiated cells within the sensory patch, demonstrating that although the otic vesicle undergoes morphogenesis and cells do extensively proliferate, progenitors do not rearrange within the epithelium during early stages of hair cell differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed maintenance of relative positions.

claim: The inner ear comprises two distinct functional modalities (vestibular and acoustic) carried out by different SAG populations.
source: The inner ear comprises two distinct functional modalities –vestibular and acoustic- carried out by different SAG populations.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about inner ear function.

claim: Place and time of neuroblast delamination are important for their allocation within the SAG.
source: Here we show the importance of place and time of neuroblast delamination in their allocation within the SAG
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings from the lineage analysis.

claim: Delamination place confers position along the AP axis of the SAG and therefore function.
source: Delamination place confers position along the AP axis of the SAG, and therefore function, most probably as the result of the integration of patterning signals involved in the emergence of the different domains (Maier and Whitfield, 2014; Radosevic et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed relationship between delamination place and SAG position, with supporting citations.

claim: Delamination time prefigures the relative position of early-delaminated neuroblasts vs. late-delaminated ones and the gradient of neuronal differentiation within the SAG.
source: Additionally, delamination time prefigures the relative position of early-delaminated neuroblasts vs. late-delaminated ones and therefore, the gradient of neuronal differentiation within the SAG.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings from the lineage analysis.

claim: An epithelial neuroblast needs to integrate spatial (its position in the epithelium) and temporal (its time of delamination) information for its final allocation within the SAG.
source: Consequently, an epithelial neuroblast will need to integrate spatial (its position in the epithelium) and temporal (its time of delamination) information for its final allocation within the SAG.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed importance of both spatial and temporal cues.

claim: Auditory neurons, which innervate the posterior macula, accumulate later than the vestibular neurons.
source: Given that auditory neurons, which innervate the PM, accumulate later than the vestibular neurons (Sapède and Pujades, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: It is possible that the majority of neuroblasts becoming auditory neurons may delaminate from posterior domains.
source: it is possible that the majority of neuroblasts becoming auditory neurons may delaminate from posterior domains, since no specific increase in cell proliferation has been observed at later stages in the posterior part of the SAG (Vemaraju et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the timing of auditory neuron accumulation and a cited observation.

claim: The knowledge of how the gradient of neuronal differentiation within the SAG is built up helps the comprehension of its differential gene expression pattern according to the neuronal differentiation state.
source: The knowledge of how the gradient of neuronal differentiation within the SAG is built up helps the comprehension of its differential gene expression pattern according to the neuronal differentiation state (Zecca et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings, with a supporting citation.

claim: During 18-30 hpf, a big proportion of epithelial neuroblasts delaminate.
source: Interesting to note is that during a relatively short period of time, 18-30 hpf, a big proportion of epithelial neuroblasts delaminate.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the observed delamination dynamics.

claim: The dramatic remodeling of the neurosensory progenitor domain may lead to changes in the exposure of progenitor domains to sources of signals.
source: This drives a dramatic remodeling of the neurosensory progenitor domain that may lead to changes in the exposure of progenitor domains to sources of signals, such as Shh from the floor plate and the ventral neural tube.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential consequences of progenitor domain remodeling.

claim: The loss of epithelial cells by delamination is probably compensated for by the active proliferation in the dorsal non-sensory territory to keep the homeostasis of the organ.
source: This loss of epithelial cells is probably compensated for by the active proliferation in the dorsal non-sensory territory in order to keep the homeostasis of the organ.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed proliferation patterns and cell loss.

claim: The study provides the dynamic map of neurosensory progenitors based on in vivo cell lineage studies.
source: Finally, we provide the dynamic map of neurosensory progenitors based on in vivo cell lineage studies supplying a global and temporal perspective to previous otic neurosensory lineage analyses, which were mainly focused on the spatial dynamics of gene expression (Durruthy-Durruthy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's contribution, with a citation to prior work.

claim: The findings establish a ground to further explore intrinsic vs. extrinsic models for cell fate determination.
source: Therefore, our findings establish a ground to further explore intrinsic vs. extrinsic models for cell fate determination, and will contribute to the mechanistic understanding of the developmental gene regulatory networks.

claim: The study reconstructed the neurosensory lineage of the inner ear by imaging zebrafish embryos in vivo over an extended timespan.
source: Here, we provide the neurosensory lineage reconstruction of a complex sensory organ, the inner ear, by imaging zebrafish embryos in vivo over an extended timespan, combining cell tracing and cell fate marker expression over time.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's approach.

claim: The study delivers the first dynamic map of early neuronal and sensory progenitor pools in the whole otic vesicle.
source: We deliver the first dynamic map of early neuronal and sensory progenitor pools in the whole otic vesicle.

claim: The otic vesicle case exemplifies a generic morphogenetic process where spatial and temporal cues regulate cell fate and functional organization of the rudiment of the definitive organ.
source: Therefore, the otic vesicle case exemplifies a generic morphogenetic process where spatial and temporal cues regulate cell fate and functional organization of the rudiment of the definitive organ.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the broader implications of the findings.
